en: The Sūtra on the King of Valiantness of All Dharmas Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dhammarakṣita of Kasmīra during the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
He was accompanied by a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

Formerly, they had all been matted-hair brahmins, with Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and others as their leaders; all were great arhats—whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, whose minds were liberated and whose wisdom was liberated, whose hearts were tamed, supple, autonomous, and unimpeded, who were like great elephants (mahānāga) having accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and attained right liberation, having mastered all dharmas and reached the other shore—with the sole exception of the Venerable Ānanda.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, when the World-Honored One was proclaiming the precepts, he sat cross-legged in an open space, surrounded by a great assembly who paid him homage with reverence and respect.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly who had not long been ordained and had just received full precepts. On that very day, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined, gazing up at him, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have not long since gone forth into homelessness today and have already received full ordination; yet, regarding the matters of this renunciation, lingering doubts remain unresolved. I only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain them for me.
How is it that a bhikṣu receives the faithful offerings of others without being deluded?
Having received such offerings, how can he further fulfill his debt of gratitude to the donor?
And for a son of good family who has conceived pure faith and resolved to leave the household life, how can he fully accomplish the Dharma for which he aspires?
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he spoke again in verse:
"I have not long been ordained, And have already received full precepts;
I have not yet understood this matter— I only pray that you will compassionately explain it."
"How does one receive the offerings of the faithful and achieve ultimate, pure retribution?
Having left the home life with a faithful mind, how does one fulfill all one's aspirations?
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes three dharmas, he will be free from delusion when receiving the faithful offerings of others;
having received them, he can purify them and fulfill his debt of gratitude;
and for those sons of good family who have left the home life out of faith, all the dharmas they aspire to shall be fully attained."
What are the three?
First, entering the ranks of the Saṃgha;
second, diligently cultivating the activities of the Saṃgha.
Third, one attains the excellent benefits of the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣu can accomplish these three dharmas, he will not be deluded when receiving the faithful offerings of others;
having received them, he is then able to remain pure and fully repay the debt.
"Those who leave the household life with faith shall have their aspirations fulfilled.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there be one who enters the ranks of the Saṃgha, And exerts themselves diligently in the deeds of the Saṃgha,"
Having attained the excellent benefits of the Saṅgha, they are in harmony with their own minds.
Such individuals as these are fully able to repay the faithful offerings made to them;
they shall completely fulfill all the dharmas that were the aspirations of their renunciation.
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has now briefly explained this meaning, yet I still do not understand it."
I only pray that the World-Honored One will graciously grant a detailed exposition:
how does a bhikṣu enter into the ranks of the Saṃgha?
How does a bhikṣu diligently cultivate the works of the Saṃgha?
"How does a bhikṣu obtain the excellent benefits of the Saṃgha?
He then spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"How does one enter the number of the Saṃgha?"
Are you diligent and progressive in the monastic life?
Have you attained the wholesome benefits of the Saṃgha?
Please deign to explain this in detail for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised this bhikṣu:
“Excellent, excellent!
You are able to inquire about this meaning.”
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well, and I shall explain for you the number of the Saṃgha, the activities of the Saṃgha, and the excellent benefits of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣu received this permission and, thirsting with longing, desired to hear it.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The four who have entered the paths and the four who have attained the fruits are called the Saṃgha. They are constantly praised by the world; among humans and the eight classes of beings, they are revered with palms joined, and among devas and humans, they are the unsurpassed field of merit."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"I now declare the four stages of progress and the four fruits of attainment;
these are called the Saṃgha, the unsurpassed field of merit."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
What is the work of the Saṃgha?

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path—this is called the work of the Saṃgha."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Always diligently practicing vigor, The most excellent Eightfold Noble Path—
In this way one enters The Sangha of the four pairs above."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus!
What is called the 'excellent benefit' of the Saṃgha?
It refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa."
What are the four?
They are the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship—these are called the benefits of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The great being’s excellent benefit is this: they enter the ranks of the Saṃgha;
possessing the four fruits of the śramaṇa, they are then able to fully repay their debt of gratitude.”
At that time, having heard these words, the bhikṣu spoke as follows:

"As the Buddha has taught, if there is a bhikṣu who is counted among the Saṃgha, diligently cultivates the works of the Saṃgha, and attains the wholesome benefits of the Saṃgha—such a person is indeed able to receive all offerings of faith;
he is free from delusion, and having received them, he is fully capable of repaying the kindness of those offerings."
"World-Honored One, those who leave the home life with faith have their aspirations fulfilled.

If there is a son of good family who resolves upon the Great Vehicle and seeks all-knowledge, and leaves the home life out of pure faith, will such a person be counted among the Saṃgha, diligently cultivate the works of the Saṃgha, and receive the benefits of the Saṃgha?"
The Buddha said:
"Monks! Excellent, excellent!"
"You possess great wisdom to be able to pose such a subtle and excellent question.
Today, for the sake of bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to gods and humans, you have been able to ask the Tathāgata about such a profound meaning."
Again he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Hold fast with mindfulness!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
"I wish and desire to hear it.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain it well and in detail.
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! If there are people who resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind, practice the Mahāyāna, and seek all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), yet out of faith leave the household life—such persons do not enter the number of the Saṃgha, do not cultivate the deeds of the Saṃgha, and do not obtain the benefits of the Saṃgha.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Not included within the ranks of the Saṃgha, not diligently practicing the works of the Saṃgha,
and not attaining the wholesome benefits of the Saṃgha— this is the cultivation of bodhi."
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Tathāgata permit such a person as this to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and accept the faithful offerings of others?”
World-Honored One!

Such a person does not enter the ranks of the Saṃgha, does not apply themselves to the work of the Saṃgha, and does not obtain the benefits of the Saṃgha; how then can they fulfill their repayment for the kindness of the gift?
The Buddha said,
"Bhikṣu! You should not now ask such a question."
The bhikṣu spoke again:

"If such a person does not enter the number of the Saṃgha, does not exert themselves in the affairs of the Saṃgha, and does not obtain the benefits of the Saṃgha, how can they fulfill the debt of gratitude for the donor's gift?"
The Buddha said:
"Stop, stop! There is no need to ask further."
As with the first request, so it was for the second and third.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Since you have requested three times, how could I not speak?"

Having spoken these words, he emitted from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows a ray of light through his supernormal power. Its brilliance blazed intensely with hundreds of thousands of colors, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm. All places of deep darkness and gloom where forms had never before been seen were made brilliantly clear. The sentient beings within the great oceans—namely fish, turtles, wild beasts, *māras*, dragon kings, and dragon maidens; various *asuras* and *asura* maidens; various *garuḍas* and *garuḍa* maidens—all such multitudes received this light. Their hearts were startled and their hair stood on end as they marveled at this unprecedented wonder.

That light also illuminated the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; as well as the Brahmā Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Ābhāsvara-svabhāva Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Parītta-bṛhatphala Heaven, the Apramāṇa-bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

This tuft of white hair between his eyebrows shines everywhere, even throughout the trichiliocosm; from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha heavens, there is no place that is not brilliantly illuminated.

When these devas had witnessed the Tathāgata’s radiance and his supernormal transformations, they each came to where the Buddha was, paying him respectful offerings, honoring and praising him; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to one side, and stood with palms joined.

At that time, there were also immeasurable bhikṣus traveling through various countries who, having encountered this light, all gathered together at the place where the Buddha was. With reverence, they made offerings, honored, and praised him; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to one side, and stood with palms joined.

At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all witnessed such miraculous transformations and supernormal powers. Having seen them, they conceived pure faith in the Buddha; they immediately went to where the Buddha was, and with reverence, making offerings, honoring, and praising him, they prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and remained there with palms joined.

Even as far as the trichiliocosm—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all such great assemblies beheld the supernatural transformations of the Tathāgata; each approached the presence of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to pay respect, make offerings, honor, and praise him. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and remained there with palms joined.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Today, immeasurable bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—all the great assemblies—have gathered together;

as have the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Akaniṣṭha devas, all of whom are harmoniously seated before the Buddha.
"For what reason has the Tathāgata emitted this light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows?
We only pray that, out of compassion, you will explain its cause and conditions.
At that time, Śāriputra spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Many sentient beings, numbering in the tens of millions (*nayuta*),
have seen this great supernatural transformation and have all come together to assemble.
For what reason do you emit this radiance and gather this great multitude?”
"I only pray that you will deign to show compassion and explain the causes for this.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
"This bhikṣu has not long been ordained; having received full precepts, he came and asked me this."
“World-Honored One!

If there are those who resolve upon the Mahāyāna mind, seeking all-knowledge, shaving off their hair and beards to leave the household life and cultivate the Way, how should they properly receive all offerings of faith?
Having received them, how can they surely repay the merit of such giving?”
"If a son of good family gives rise to faith, leaves the household life, and trains in the Way, will his aspirations not all be fulfilled before long?
"Śāriputra! For these reasons, such a great multitude as this has gathered together."
Śāriputra said:
"Now is precisely the right time; I only pray that the Tathāgata will analyze and expound upon such a meaning.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If I were to explain this meaning now, many hundreds of thousands of sentient beings would give rise to doubt and confusion in their minds.
Why is this? Because the supernatural powers and penetrations of these great nāgas are inconceivable."
The fearless lion’s roar of these teachers is also inconceivable;
the dharma-realm of these great beings is likewise inconceivable, Śāriputra!
The dharma-realm of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is inconceivable; it cannot be believed or understood by any ordinary beings, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas. Śāriputra!
"Because the Tathāgata perceives these various causes and conditions, he remains silent and does not speak.
At that time, Śāriputra made his request three times, yet the Tathāgata remained silent and did not grant permission.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Within this great assembly, there are already immeasurable and boundless bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, who have long since conceived pure faith in the presence of the Buddha. We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for these sentient beings, will analyze and expound upon such meanings.”
Again, before the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
“Excellent, O Unsurpassed Honored One!
I pray that you will deign to show compassion And extensively explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas The merits of the *uṣṇīṣa*.”
"There are sentient beings who, with deep aspiration, seek awakening;
having already developed a heart of profound and wholesome desire for this Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“A bodhisattva mahāsattva should receive the respectful offerings and veneration of all devas, humans, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.”
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva does not fully repay the kindness of those who give. Why is this?
Śāriputra! This is because the bodhisattva mahāsattva has already fundamentally purified himself through the completion of the retribution for his giving. Śāriputra!

Suppose a bodhisattva-mahāsattva were to receive daily all the food and clothing offered by all sentient beings; even if each sentient being’s offering of food were as large as Mount Sumeru and each garment were sufficient to cover the four continents, and he were to receive such food and clothing from all sentient beings every single day, he would still be able to remain pure and fully repay the kindness of those donors.
Why is this? Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas are the foremost fields of merit among all sentient beings; they are those who should receive the offerings of the world.
Śāriputra!

Do you see those great wealthy people in the world who possess many precious treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musaragalva, and agate—as well as various soft furnishings? These include those of the great Kṣatriya clans, the great Brāhmaṇa clans, the great householder families, the minor kings of scattered territories, and the wheel-turning sage-kings who have accomplished the seven treasures and exercise sovereignty among men.

Whether it be the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the sons of the gods of Yama, the sons of the gods of Tuṣita, the sons of the gods of Nirmāṇarati, or the sons of the gods of Paranirmita-vaśavartin;
the Brahmā Sahāmpati King and the other devas of the form and formless realms;
or those who have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or pratyekabuddha;
Śāriputra, if it were not for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—
and likewise for all such multitudes— they would all appear in the world only through the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva’s teaching and transformation.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva resolves their mind to practice the path to enlightenment, they shall next attain Buddhahood and realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Once it is accomplished, you shall further turn the Wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by any in the entire world—whether śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the Brahmā King, or the Māra Pāpīyān.

"At that time, there will be immeasurable sentient beings who, having heard this Dharma, shall attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and the fruit of *arhat*;

some shall resolve for the mind of a *pratyekabuddha*; and some shall resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Upon hearing the teaching on giving, they will diligently practice it; by the causes and conditions of such giving, they will be born into great clans of *kṣatriyas*, great clans of *brāhmaṇas*, great families of householders, or royal families of minor kings, or as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) endowed with the seven treasures, possessing sovereignty among men.

Upon hearing the teaching on the observance of precepts, they will firmly uphold them; by these causes and conditions, they will be born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven."
Hearing the teaching on the four immeasurable minds and practicing in accordance with them, one is born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) by reason of these causes and conditions;

hearing the four meditative absorptions of emptiness (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and practicing in accordance with them, one is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) by reason of these causes and conditions.
Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that it is entirely due to the causes and conditions of bodhisattvas that all wholesome dharmas appear in the world. Śāriputra!

For example, by the power of the merit of the Dragon King Anavatapta, four great rivers flow from his lake—the Ganges in the east, the Sindhu in the south, the Vakṣu in the west, and the Sītā in the north. These four great rivers flow out toward the four directions and empty into the four great oceans.
The Gaṅgā, with its retinue of five hundred rivers, flows into the eastern ocean;
the Sindhu, with its retinue of five hundred rivers, flows into the southern ocean;
the Vakṣu, with its retinue of five hundred rivers, flows into the western ocean;
The Sītā’s retinue consists of five hundred rivers that flow into the Northern Sea.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Do these four great rivers, flowing out from the four directions and successively entering the four great oceans, bring benefit to sentient beings in those four directions?
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
It truly brings great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, namely those who fly and those who run—humans and non-humans alike.”
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!

The various fields of rice, wheat, millet, and beans near this riverbank will also receive moistening; thus, these fields will yield abundant grain and wheat, further benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, namely the birds and beasts, humans and non-humans alike.”
“Śāriputra, what do you think?
From what do these four great oceans arise?”
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
These four great oceans all arise from the four rivers.”
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
"What do you think?
Do these four great oceans provide any benefit to sentient beings?"
Śāriputra said: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”

This ocean is truly able to benefit immeasurable and boundless sentient beings—namely those of both terrestrial and aquatic natures, such as large and small fish, wild beasts, *māras*, turtles, tortoises, frogs, geese, wild ducks, and mandarin ducks—and it also serves as a dwelling place for countless other species of aquatic creatures.
“Śāriputra! This great ocean further serves as a dwelling place for other beings, namely the nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas.

It also produces immeasurable and boundless treasures to benefit all humans and non-humans—namely pearls, conch shells, jade, coral, lapis lazuli, and blue beryl—as well as various other kinds of precious gems, all of which are utilized by sentient beings to bring them benefit.”
Śāriputra, what do you think?
From what do these four great oceans arise?
Śāriputra said:
“World-Honored One!
These oceans all originate from Lake Anavatapta.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
The Naga King Anavatapta is free from the three fears."
What are the three?
First, the garuḍa;
second, hot sand.
Third, when other dragons engage in sexual desire, they take the form of snakes; however, the Dragon King Anavatapta does not have such a thing.
Śāriputra, the palace where the Dragon King Anavatapta dwells is a place inhabited by those who practice dhyāna and possess supernormal powers.
“Śāriputra!
If there are those who can abide in this state, you should know that they too shall attain freedom from affliction.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is truly rare.
The palace of the Dragon King Anavatapta has accomplished such supreme and virtuous merit that not even one of the three fears exists there, let alone all three.”
If there are sentient beings dwelling in this palace, they likewise fully possess these three things that are not [otherwise] present.

If this is the dwelling place of one who possesses supernatural powers and virtuous reflection, then from this place the four great rivers will surely emerge, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings.

For this reason, the waters of the four great oceans serve as resources for all sentient beings and act as their dwelling places—namely, for those born from eggs, such as various birds, as well as other beasts, humans, and non-humans.
“World-Honored One!
This Lake Anavatapta is endowed with such immeasurable merits.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Just as the Naga King Anavatapta is by nature free from the three fears, so too is the Bodhisattva by nature free from the three fears.
What are these three?
First, the fear of hell;..."
Second, the fear of animals;
third, the fear of hungry ghosts. Śāriputra!

Just as the four great rivers emerge from Lake Anavatapta to benefit boundless and immeasurable sentient beings, so too does the bodhisattva gather in sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*):
first, giving; second, kind speech; [third, beneficial conduct; and fourth, common purpose].
Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is cooperation. Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas benefit sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Śāriputra, just as the four great oceans emerge from Lake Anavatapta, so too does the Bodhisattva: from the bodhicitta emerges the ocean of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Śāriputra! Just as the great ocean serves as a place of peace, security, and happiness for all sentient beings,
so it is, Śāriputra.
The knowledge of all modes is likewise so: it serves as a place of peace, security, and happiness for sentient beings within the three realms.
What are these three realms?
They are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Śāriputra! It is entirely due to the Bodhisattva’s wandering and teaching that all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm are enabled to attain peace and happiness.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if there are bodhisattvas who appear in the world and practice the bodhisattva path, they receive a prediction of enlightenment because of their cultivation of that path.

Having received the prediction of enlightenment, they shall then attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and turn the wheel of Dharma, which cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Brahmā kings, or Māra Pāpīyas in all the worlds.
Upon hearing this, there arose the fourfold assembly—namely, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

By virtue of these causes and conditions, these four assemblies experienced various kinds of subtle and wondrous happiness, as well as the bliss of detachment from desire, among both devas and humans.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
From what cause do such dharmas as these arise?
Śāriputra said:
"All arise through the causes and conditions of the bodhisattva.
"Śāriputra! [the Buddha continued.]
"What do you think?
From what, furthermore, do the phenomena bound to the three realms arise?
Śāriputra replied:
"It also emerges through the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"What do you think?"
"In this regard, among all dharmas, is there perhaps even a single dharma that can repay the kindness bestowed by a bodhisattva?
Śāriputra replied,
"No, World-Honored One."
Why is this? Because it is due to the emergence of such dharmas as these from the Bodhisattva into the world,
World-Honored One!

For example, suppose there were a person who possessed abundant treasures; out of a compassionate heart, they bestowed the immeasurable treasures from their own storehouses and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of goods upon the poor.

In this manner, they successively provide for two people, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, and hundreds of thousands of millions of people; thus, even unto immeasurable sentient beings, both those with form and those without form, they relinquish all their possessions and wealth to bestow upon such immeasurable beings. Furthermore, they eliminate their fears, bondage, flogging, scourging, rebukes, and [rebirth in] the various evil realms, while simultaneously establishing them in the bliss of humans and devas.
Now, suppose there were a man among this assembly who took a single coin, broke it into a hundred parts, and wished to repay the kindness of that person's gift with just one part of that coin.
"Bhagavān, what do you think?
This great donor has brought immense benefit to all sentient beings; if this person now wishes to repay that kindness with but a single coin, would he truly be able to repay it?"
"No, Śāriputra," he replied. Śāriputra said:

“The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: just as that wealthy man benefits all immeasurable sentient beings and, for the sake of severing and extinguishing all evils, repays their kindness with a single coin.”
World-Honored One!

It is the same for one who practices the Mahāyāna: by means of the various kinds of pleasures at will experienced by such immeasurable sentient beings, they wish to repay the kindness of the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve, yet it would be like that person repaying the benefactor’s kindness with a single coin.
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
You now act in accordance with my practice."
Śāriputra!

If all sentient beings, throughout a hundred lifetimes, a thousand lifetimes, ten thousand lifetimes, or even hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes—exhausting their physical life span in each and every one of those lives—were to offer up their bodies, skin, flesh, marrow, bones, tendons, and veins to a Bodhisattva, they still could not repay even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-billionth part, or even a fraction beyond the reach of calculation of the kindness of such a Bodhisattva.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
I observe that among all the great assemblies of humans, devas, and asuras, there is none who can repay the kindness of this bodhisattva.
Except for those sons and daughters of good family who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If there are good sons or good daughters who resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will be utilized by all immeasurable sentient beings and bring great benefit to many.
“Śāriputra! It is like the sandalwood tree that grows in Jambudvīpa: when its sprouts emerge, they can eliminate all the suffering of illness of infants, both male and female;
when its leaves emerge, they can further cure all the ailments of boys and girls.”
When the tree grows and its branches and leaves become luxuriant, providing cool shade, all sentient beings within it are able to eliminate all suffering from illness.
When its flowers bloom, they enable devas and humans to achieve happiness.

When its fruit ripens, a great radiance shines forth, illuminating the ten directions; if any sentient beings see this and give rise to mindfulness, recognizing that light, they immediately attain the cessation of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
When it perishes, there will be sentient beings who take its trunk; they shall never thereafter fear the suffering of poverty.
If they take its branches and leaves back to their homes, they will no longer suffer from hunger or thirst.

Śāriputra! This sandalwood tree appears in the world to constantly benefit sentient beings; there is never a time when it does not provide benefit. From the moment its sprouts emerge until its branches and leaves are taken home, it constantly acts for their benefit.
“Śāriputra, it is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.

When first generating the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they gather in sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu). Once that mind has been generated, their mind constantly takes the three gates of liberation as its object.”
What are the three?
Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
That which is called the growth of the tree refers to the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
The blossoming of flowers refers to the already perfected attainment of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);
the ripening of fruit refers to the Tathāgata’s entry into *parinirvāṇa*;
and the breaking of the tree refers to the fact that after *parinirvāṇa*, his bodily relics (*śarīra*) are shattered by means of supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*) into pieces like mustard seeds.

"Taking its branches and leaves and returning home" means that after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, one collects his relics and erects various stūpas and temples; when sentient beings enter within them, their decline and evil are eliminated.
Śāriputra!

For this reason, you should know that for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all roots of goodness planted by sentient beings therein shall receive their full retribution.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

If there are good men or good women who resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, it is because they wish to cause those who practice the lineage of the Buddha to succeed one another, and they also wish to ensure that the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not cut off, so as to bestow happiness upon all immeasurable sentient beings—both humans and devas—and to provide them with the untainted bliss that is free from afflictions.

Śāriputra! If there were one who could bestow upon all sentient beings the happiness of humans and devas, as well as the untainted bliss that is free from afflictions—could such a person be described by means of a simile to illustrate their likeness?
Śāriputra said:
“No, World-Honored One.
World-Honored One!”

Neither among gods, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, or Brahmās, nor among any other immeasurable multitudes, could anyone—whether in one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand million kalpas, or even for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas—ever repay the kindness of a bodhisattva’s initial resolve for enlightenment.

“Śāriputra! For this reason, if good sons and good daughters wish to attain the unsurpassed and ultimate repayment for the kindness of giving, they should resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra! If good sons or good daughters wish to repay the kindness of the Buddhas of the past, they too should likewise resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! If good sons or good daughters wish to repay the kindness of all future Tathāgatas, they too should likewise resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! If good sons or good daughters wish to repay the kindness of the Buddhas of the ten directions who are currently present, they too should likewise resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Only two kinds of people are able to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
What are these two?
First, the exhaustion of outflows;
second, the arousal of the mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Śāriputra!
"These two kinds of people are well able to make offerings to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and are well able to repay all the kindness bestowed by the Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The two kinds of people mentioned Are able to make offerings to all Buddhas."
Those known as Arhats and Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—
these are called the two persons who make offerings to all the World-Honored Ones;
within the three realms, there is no third person besides them.
If there are those who can impartially observe all phenomena,
such individuals as these are called wise ones.
Even with all manner of exquisite fivefold desires and whatever else is lovely and necessary, they remain unattached.
Even if one were to make offerings to these bodhisattvas, their kindness would still not be fully repaid.
But if one makes offerings to those who have transcended craving, to arhats in their final bodies,
and to those who have resolved for the unsurpassed mind and practice for enlightenment— [their kindness is even more immeasurable].
This is indeed the foremost, the unsurpassed field of merit.
Gods, humans, and the various Brahmās each offer what they hold dear to these Bodhisattvas,
yet even so, the Bodhisattvas do not regard it as a debt of gratitude to be repaid.
These two kinds of people have, in truth, no need for anything;
though they receive the highest offerings, their minds are free from greedy attachment.
For this reason, although one may serve them, it cannot repay their kindness.
If those wise ones in the world wish to make offerings to the Buddha,
they should resolve upon bodhicitta and practice patience.
If they wish to perform meritorious deeds, they should do so repeatedly and immeasurably.
For the sake of awakening, one should perform the unsurpassed deeds.
If one wishes to attain meditative concentration, one should cultivate the four immeasurable minds;
such a person ought to be diligent for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Those who wish to obtain all happiness and eliminate all suffering and affliction should, within the Buddha’s Dharma,
give rise to a profound and earnest aspiration and seek the unsurpassed path to its conclusion.
If you wish to behold and pay homage to the immeasurable World-Honored Ones,
you should give rise to a heart of reverence and seek the true and correct Path with profound earnestness.
If you wish to travel from one realm to immeasurable realms, [you must do so through this path].
One should give rise to diligent vigor and a deep longing for enlightenment.
Desiring to see the Buddhas of the past, one should give rise to the desire for vigor;
for the sake of enlightenment, one should practice and train in perfect accordance with the Dharma.
If you wish to swiftly behold the Buddhas of future ages,
you should likewise cultivate the path with a single-minded and sincere heart for the sake of Bodhi.
Furthermore, if you wish to behold the World-Honored Ones of the present, [you should likewise cultivate the path].
One should likewise give rise to a mind of virtuous aspiration for the sake of enlightenment;
know that such persons are supreme, extraordinary, and not inferior.
If one wishes to practice universal loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, [one should do so].
This person should apply themselves with diligence, Quickly seeking the unsurpassed path.
If they wish to cause all sentient beings To completely eliminate all suffering and affliction,
They should study unsurpassed wisdom, Without abandoning it in the interim.
If one wishes to bestow upon all sentient beings every form of happiness,
the wise person, for the sake of Bodhi, should give rise to a profound and virtuous aspiration.
If one wishes to extinguish the immeasurable evil realms of sentient beings, [one should likewise give rise to such an aspiration].
The wise should grasp the ultimate bodhicitta.
Regarding the immeasurable merits obtained by such a person,
there is no one at all who can provide a simile for them.
"That is to say, they have resolved their minds on Bodhi, desiring to accomplish the Unsurpassed Way.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How many merits are obtained by preaching this sutra now?
And how many sentient beings will resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“You should not now ask such a question.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If the Tathāgata were to speak of the matters of omniscience, it would cause many sentient beings to give rise to doubt and confusion.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and boundless supernormal powers.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
“Could the Tathāgata explain the boundaries, limits, divisions, or demarcations of space such that they could be known, calculated, or measured?
“No, World-Honored One!”
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Regarding the limits of space, there is no one who has known them, knows them now, or will know them.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The wisdom of the Buddha is likewise; it was unknown to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the past, is not known now, and will not be known in the future."
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the unsurpassed wisdom possessed by the Tathāgata is not within the sphere of activity or the realm of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra said:
"These sentient beings are truly rare; they are well able to discern unsurpassed bodhi and are thus able to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!
Just as you have said, these sentient beings are truly rare; they are well able to discern unsurpassed bodhi and are thus able to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
Śāriputra, what do you think?

Suppose all sentient beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa—whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial—were to obtain human bodies, and a single person were to instruct these people, causing them to abide securely in the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions. Śāriputra!
"What do you think?
Would this person, by reason of these causes and conditions, acquire much merit? "Very much."
“World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by such a person cannot be compared by means of analogy.

“I shall now speak: if a good man or a good woman were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, causing them to abide securely in the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, the merit they would thereby obtain would not equal that of a person who instructs and guides a single individual, causing them to attain the practice of faith.”
Śāriputra, let this matter rest for a moment.

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught all the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and caused them to attain the stage of faith-practice (śraddhā-caryā), it would not be as meritorious as someone who instructs and guides a single person so that they attain the stage of dharma-practice (dharma-caryā).
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they attain the practice of the Dharma, it would not equal someone who instructs and guides a single person so that they attain the stage of the Eight Persons (aṣṭamaka).
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa so that they attain the stage of the Eight Persons, it would not be as meritorious as someone instructing and exhorting a single person so that they attain the fruit of a Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa and cause them to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, it would not be equal to someone who instructs and guides a single person to attain the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin.
Śāriputra! Let this matter rest for now.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to teach all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they attain the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, it would not be equal to someone who instructs and exhorts a single person, causing them to attain the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If a son or daughter of good family were to teach all the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa to attain the fruit of an Anāgāmin, it would not be as meritorious as someone teaching and instructing a single person to attain the fruit of an Arhat.
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If a good man or a good woman were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they attain the fruit of arhatship, it would not be equal to someone instructing and teaching a single person so that they attain the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa to attain the state of a pratyekabuddha, it would not be as meritorious as someone who instructs and exhorts a single person to resolve their mind toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! Let this matter be set aside for a moment.

If a good man or a good woman were to instruct all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa to resolve upon bodhicitta, it would not be as meritorious as someone who instructs and exhorts a single person to attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Śāriputra! Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

If there were a son or daughter of good family who taught all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa and caused them to attain the stage of non-retrogression, it would not be equal to someone who instructs and exhorts a single person so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Śāriputra! Let this matter rest for now.

If a good man or a good woman were to teach all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), it would not equal the merit of someone who exhorts and teaches a single person to quickly achieve unsurpassed wisdom.
Śāriputra! Let this matter rest for now.

If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who taught all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa so that they might swiftly attain unsurpassed wisdom, it would not equal the merit of someone who diligently cultivates and collects such a sūtra as this.

Why is this? Because this sutra can destroy all hosts of Māras, break through the aggregates (skandhas), keep one distant from the elements (dhātus), disperse the sense bases (āyatanas), eliminate afflictions (kleśas), give rise to the pure nature, and remove all burdensome dharmas.
If one can extensively analyze and explain this *Sūtra of the Heroic King of All Dharmas* for other sentient beings, the merit obtained will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description.

“Śāriputra! Setting aside all sentient beings in a single Jambudvīpa; setting aside all sentient beings in the four continents; setting aside all sentient beings in a small thousand-world system; setting aside all sentient beings in a medium thousand-world system; setting aside all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm.”

Śāriputra! Suppose that in the east, south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and above and below—in all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all sentient beings therein, whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, whether aquatic, terrestrial, or aerial; born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation—should these sentient beings gradually and successively attain human bodies. If there were a son or daughter of good family who taught all those immeasurable sentient beings and caused them to abide securely in the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, Śāriputra!
"What do you think?
Would these sons or daughters of good family, by reason of this cause and condition, acquire much merit?
Śāriputra replied:
“Very much,
World-Honored One!
The merit obtained by this person cannot be compared by means of any analogy.”
“Śāriputra! Let this matter rest for now.”

If one were to teach the sentient beings of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, causing them to attain the stage of faith, the stage of Dharma-practice, the stage of the eight persons, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, the fruit of arhatship, the path of the pratyekabuddha, the arousal of the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, non-retrogression, the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, and the swift accomplishment of supreme, all-encompassing wisdom—it would not equal the merit obtained by someone who, using this *Sarvadharmanirdeśavīrarāja Sūtra*, analyzes and explains it extensively for other sentient beings. The merit from exhorting and transforming sentient beings in this manner is the most distinguished among the former; it is the most honorable, unsurpassed, most exquisite, most virtuous, most excellent, peerless, incomparable, and beyond match.
Śāriputra! You should know that such unsurpassed skillful means can cause a bodhisattva to practice the path to enlightenment with definitive certainty. Why is this?
Śāriputra! If there are bodhisattvas who hear this *Sarvadharmanirghoṣarāja* Sūtra, having heard it, they immediately attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

One should know that such a person can act as a field of merit for sentient beings; they are peerless and beyond compare, having attained liberation and reached the further shore. Pure, disciplined, and tranquil in *nirvāṇa*, they are true sons of the Buddha, worthy of receiving offerings. They are brave and heroic lions among men, surpassing both humans and devas; they are dragons among men and gods among gods. They are unattached, unfettered, and free from all hindrances; having accomplished what was to be done, they have perfected all tasks, being fully endowed with immeasurable merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one gives rise to the bodhicitta, One will ultimately reach the other shore;
Such great beings as these Have no doubt in their minds."
If one gives to such persons as these, one will obtain immeasurable rewards of merit.
If you wish to obtain such merit, you should resolve upon the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
Once the mind of enlightenment has been resolved upon, the mass of merit thereby obtained—
If one wished to describe even a small fraction of it, it could not be measured.
Even if one were to teach all sentient beings throughout immeasurable worlds and cause them all to abide in the five precepts,
and even further increase their practice, [it would still not equal a portion of this merit].
Though one may provide such instruction, it is not equal to the arousal of bodhicitta;
there is nothing else that can compare to it, except for the understanding of this sutra.
If one studies this scripture, that person is a fertile field of merit.
They should receive offerings from gods and humans;
being tranquil and well-subdued, if they hear this sutra, they are truly the sons of the Buddha.
They are also called those who are diligent and energetic, having attained the far shore of tranquility.
This one is the lion among gods and nāgas, and for this reason is called a Great Being;
he is also the god among gods, the most honored among all sentient beings.
If there be anyone able to proclaim such a wondrous sūtra as this,
"This one shall then be named the Unsurpassed among Men.
After the Buddha had spoken this verse, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
It is unprecedented!
World-Honored One, within this *Sarvadharmavikrāntagāmin-sūtra*, you have briefly expounded all the instructions for bodhisattvas.
World-Honored One!
Although Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the deeds appropriate for a bodhisattva for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, it remains difficult for them to achieve unexcelled bodhi;
yet now, World-Honored One, you have taught in this sutra that the unexcelled path is not difficult.
World-Honored One!
These sentient beings have swiftly attained excellent benefit—the foremost benefit.
World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who hear this sutra, read and recite it with thorough mastery, and explain it extensively for others, you should know that such persons have already set out toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!
This wondrous sutra—may the Tathāgata deign to expound it once more.”
Why is this? As I understand the meaning and principles of what the Buddha has taught, among all the sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Buddhas of the past, this sūtra is the most preeminent;
among all the sūtras and dharmas that will be spoken by the Buddhas of the future, this sūtra is likewise the most excellent.
"Whatever unsurpassed wheels of Dharma are being turned by the Buddhas of the ten directions in the present, this sutra is likewise preeminent among them.
World-Honored One!

I have also previously spoken immeasurable sūtras and their words, and I have also heard immeasurable sūtras and their meanings and flavors from the Tathāgata; yet I have never before heard a sūtra such as this."
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that out of compassion you will repeatedly and extensively expound such a sutra as this.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata himself knows this meaning; whenever sentient beings give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, at that time I shall explain it extensively for them and thereby gather them in.”
Śāriputra! All such things are known by the Tathāgata alone; they are not within the reach or comprehension of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others. Śāriputra!

As I now preach this subtle and wondrous sūtra, eighty-four thousand Brahmās and humans, as well as thirty-six billion devas of the desire realm who had not yet resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, have all now resolved their minds upon it;
thirty billion devas have attained the dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*);
and immeasurable and innumerable devas of the causal stages, nāgas, and spirits who had not yet resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, have all now resolved their minds upon it.
“Śāriputra!
It is because I see such beneficial purposes that, from time to time, I extensively proclaim such sūtras as these.

At that time, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of beings in the assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—who joined their palms, knelt for a long time, and gazed up at the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes.

At that time, the Tathāgata smiled with a serene countenance—for it is the constant law of all Buddhas not to smile without cause—and having smiled, he emitted various rays of light from his face: blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and the color of crystal. These lights illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds, reaching as far upward as the Brahma Heaven; they circled his body three times and then entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The Buddhas do not smile without cause or condition.
World-Honored One,
what is the cause and condition for your smile now?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“Do you now see these immeasurable and innumerable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—who stand before me with palms joined in reverence, gazing up at me without blinking?”
“I have seen them, World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This great assembly wishes with longing to hear of the unsurpassed practice cultivated by bodhisattvas.”
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata knows, in accordance with reality, the thoughts and the conduct of all sentient beings; therefore, I shall now speak of them for you. Śāriputra!
If a person does not perceive the mind of the past, present, or future, this is called the practice of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if one does not perceive the nature or conceptualization of the aggregates, does not crave the elements, and does not cling to the sense bases,
this is called the dharma practiced by a bodhisattva.
"This is indeed what has been taught by the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening.
When he had finished speaking these teachings on the practices of bodhisattvas, the Buddha-world of three thousandfold great thousandfold worlds shook in six ways.
At that time, Pāpīyān and his retinue, residing in the palace of Māra, were struck with terror and trembling; they immediately fell to the ground and each spoke a verse before the Buddha:
“We and our retinue, Are now utterly destroyed;
All have fallen to the ground, And none shall return.”
If the Buddha were to expound this scripture in its entirety without omission,
it could destroy the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of the aggregates, and the Māra of death,
causing their power to perish so that not a trace remains.
By hearing that all phenomena are empty, the power of Māra is thereby weakened;
by attaining the wisdom of non-self, the Māra of Death retreats and disperses.
Because one has realized the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, one will no longer undergo future births.
At that time, Pāpīyas spoke again in verse:
“Excellent is your diligent exertion, O supreme Great Dragon!
Now I, together with my retinue, All undergo immeasurable suffering.”
“I only pray that with a face of compassionate grace, you will take pity on me and grant me consolation;
may I, by means of this cause, not enter the gate of death.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke a verse to Pāpīyas:
“Pāpīyān, you and your retinue, If you wish to escape the gateway of death,
You should give rise to deep faith and a pure mind Toward this sutra.
Within all the worlds, There are few who are able to believe.”
"Therefore, you should now believe, accept, and practice this.
At that time, having heard these verses, Pāpīyān leaped for joy and suddenly vanished.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the bhikṣu who had asked the question, and the entire assembly—including other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, humans, and non-humans—heard what the Buddha had said and were all filled with joy. They praised him, saying, "Excellent! and having paid their respects, they departed.
